title: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

sense.text:
“Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ”. “For by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.” No flesh is justified by the works of the law: that is what Paul said, and everything turns on which law he means.

The works of the law here are the same works of the law in Galatians 3:2, 3:5 and 3:10, and the same law Hebrews 9 and 10 speak of: the law of sacrifice, the offering up of animals. Faith in Christ, in his death, is what justifies, not the blood of animals.

“O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you”. Pharisees and scribes had come into the body of Christ. They seemed to be believers, but they were false brethren brought in unawares, infiltrating the churches and deceiving them, spreading the doctrine of animal sacrifice as more important than Christ’s sacrifice. That is who bewitched them.

“Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?” Did you receive the Spirit, the understanding of Christ, by the works of the law, or by hearing and understanding the faith?
“Having begun in the Spirit”, as believers in Christ, “are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” By the flesh means by the law: the flesh of the animals. It is the same thing.
“Have ye suffered so many things in vain?” Have you suffered following Christ for nothing?
Right back to verse 2: he that “worketh miracles among you”, does he do it “by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?”
“Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.” They which are of faith are “the children of Abraham”: the Israelites.

God would “justify the heathen through faith”: the heathen are the Gentiles: the northern kingdom, the Israelites scattered abroad. “In thee shall all nations be blessed”, because all Israel would be scattered among all nations and blessed there by Christ’s death.

“So then they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.” Abraham’s faith was accounted to him before any sacrificing. He believed God, believed the promises, believed he would inherit land and receive a son in his old age, and his faith was accounted first and foremost. Faith must come before anything else.

“For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse”. The works of the law are in verse 2, in verse 5, in Galatians 2:16, and here again. The curse is condemnation and death: cursed be he that does this, cursed be he that does that, cursed be he that commits adultery, that kills, that steals, that bears false witness, that disrespects his mother and father, that worships idols. There is no repentance for those things.

“Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them”: all things means the commandments coupled with sacrificing. In Paul’s time the temple still stood and people were still accustomed to offering up animals. But the Galatians did not come into this truth by offering up animals. They came in because they heard that Christ died for them, redeemed them from all the sins the animals could not atone for, granted them eternal life if they keep his commandments, and grafted them back in with their brothers, the southern kingdom.

The northern kingdom, the Gentiles, the scattered Israelites, were heavily rooted in idolatry, and under the old covenant idolatry was immediate condemnation. No animal in the temple could atone for idolatry or fornication. So if you put yourself under that law of sacrifice, you are under the curse, condemned, because what you are guilty of could not be atoned for under the Mosaic law.

precepts.why:
“Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image”. “And all the people shall answer and say, Amen.” Death. Israel agreed to it: if we break these commandments, we are destroyed, cursed.

One after another: “Cursed be he that setteth light by his father or his mother”, that dishonours them; “Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour’s landmark”; “Cursed be he that maketh the blind to wander out of the way”; “Cursed be he that perverteth the judgment of the stranger, fatherless, and widow”; “Cursed be he that lieth with his father’s wife”; “Cursed be he that lieth with any manner of beast”, and no animal atones for that; with his sister, with his mother in law; “Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly”; “Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person”. Every time, “all the people shall say, Amen.” They agreed to being cursed if they violated these laws.

“Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them.” That is where Paul is quoting from in Galatians 3:10.

All of these go to morality: civil and moral law, how you deal with your brother, your father, your sister, your neighbour. They go right back to loving thy neighbour as thyself.

“In which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect”. The sacrifices did not make those who offered them perfect. We were sinful by nature, and the animals did not help us. They were a stepping stone leading us to Christ.

They “stood only in meats and drinks”, meat offerings and drink offerings, “and divers washings”, purifications, baptisms, the same thing, “and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.” The sacrifices were imposed on us: we were bound to continue in all the works of that law or be cursed, until Christ came and ended it. The reformation is Christ dying on the cross and becoming our high priest.

“A greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands” is the one in heaven, which the tabernacle on earth was modeled after. When Christ died he went up to the temple in the heavens and offered himself for our sins: “Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.” Under the animals, redemption had to be sought daily, constantly, and it could never make us perfect. Christ died once so the animals are no longer needed. The temple still stood and by habit they still sacrificed, but Paul was already setting them on the path: after a while the temple will be destroyed and the priests gone. What will you do then? If you are still bound to that, you condemn yourself.

“The ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean” is purification, the water of separation: baptism. They would take the ashes of an heifer and hyssop, put it in the water and sprinkle the people, washing them physically. John got that practice from the Levites, being a Levite, and did it outside the temple in the Jordan, paving the way for Christ, who would wash away our sins with the word of God. “How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” Christ’s blood supersedes baptism, physical water. It is better, much more, for you baptism people out there who want somebody to wash away your sins in the damn tub.

“For the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament”. Who was under the first testament? The Israelites. Christ died to redeem those who sinned under the first testament, and that is the “us” of verse 12: not all nations, not everybody. “They which are called”, the Israelites, “might receive the promise of eternal inheritance.”

“For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator.” The old testament is the will and testament of Christ, from his beginning to his end, and everything written in it he must fulfil, particularly his death. When a man dies, what is in his will must be carried out; while he lives, it cannot be. Once Christ died on the cross he set his will in motion: all the prophecies, us going into slavery in ships, being scattered among all the nations under different identities, America’s inception out of Rome, the seals opening, Rome coming to destroy Jerusalem as Daniel shows, and his coming back to get us and save us. “For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth.” So if we are still under the old covenant, Christ would have to die a second time. That is how stupid that doctrine is.

“Neither the first testament was dedicated without blood.” Moses “took the blood of calves and of goats, with water, and scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book, and all the people”: the purification again, the baptism, with blood. “This is the blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you”, and we all said Amen. We agreed.

“And almost all things are by the law purged with blood”. Almost, because some sins no animal could be offered for: idolatry, bestiality, homosexuality, breaking the Sabbath, murder, adultery. Those got death. If you was out here doing Diddy stuff, you got death; out on Epstein island, you were finished under Mosaic law, no atoning for the witchcraft, the baby eating, the rape. And the poor who could bring only flour still had an animal sacrificed for them: blood had to be shed for everyone.

“Without shedding of blood is no remission.” No forgiveness, no atonement, no justification, no redemption. Remission means your judgment is put on pause, halted, because the animal dies in your stead. That is why it is called a scapegoat: you escaped death by the animal dying for you. Like cancer going into remission, it stops spreading. Without that, for almost all things, you got straight death.

“For the law having a shadow of good things to come” is the same law as Hebrews 9: the blood of bulls and of calves, the law of sacrifice. Chapter 10 does not change the context. Sacrifice is part of the commandments, but here it is primarily animal sacrifice.

Those sacrifices “which they offered year by year continually” could never “make the comers thereunto perfect”: the priests, who sacrificed for themselves and then for the people. Christ died one time and granted us eternal redemption; under Moses we offered for redemption year by year. If the sacrifices made you perfect, “then would they not have ceased to be offered?” Imperfect people offering up animals made the sacrifice imperfect too. The animal dying on your behalf was to put fear in you: damn, that could have been me, let me stop sinning. But we sin anyway, because we are sinful by nature; David said in sin did his mother conceive him. “There is a remembrance again made of sins every year.” “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins”, because the carnal nature that covers us, this flesh, keeps sinning over and over.

“Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me”: Paul is quoting Psalms 40, Christ speaking through David about what he would do when he came on the earth: his body prepared to be the sacrifice. “In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure”: thou wouldest not and had no pleasure are the same thing said twice. God kept saying over and over, I don’t care about sacrifice. It was a stepping stone, a placeholder for Christ. “Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.”

The sacrifices “are offered by the law”: the same works of the law Paul speaks of in Galatians 2:16, 3:2, 3:5 and 3:10. The works of the law is sacrifice. “He taketh away the first”, when he died, “that he may establish the second”: the second covenant, the new covenant. “By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” He did it once, in the temple in the heavens not made with hands, and that was it. If you are under the old covenant, he has to do it a second time. That is how stupid that is.

“And every priest standeth daily”, “But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God”. When he left us and went up into the heavens, he sat down at the right hand of his Father in his own throne. People say Christ has no throne, standing up there in the corner on punishment, legs hurting all day: that is the dumbest thing ever heard. The angels around him have thrones and the Christ has to stand there? A king with no throne makes no damn sense. “From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool”: his enemies are not his footstool yet, so until then he is sitting at the right hand of his Father. Simplicity in Christ.

“After those days” is now, the new covenant: “I will put my laws into their hearts, and in their minds will I write them”. He will give us a new body, and in that new body we can accept the laws of God and keep them perfectly, in the kingdom. “And their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.” “Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin.” The remission came from Christ dying on the cross, and after that there is no need to offer animals anymore. You could if you wanted, because the temple was still standing, but there was no need: he granted us eternal redemption by offering his body once for all.

sense.text: “But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God”: the law of sacrifice again. Where remission of sins is, there is no more offering for sin. “It is evident: for, The just shall live by faith.” Paul is quoting Habakkuk 2:4.

precepts.why:
“Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him”: Esau. His soul is not right, by spirit, by nature, by biology. That nation is not right at all in the spirit or in their heads; there is something wrong with them. “But the just shall live by his faith.” That is where Paul got it.

Abraham’s faith was counted for righteousness. His faith came first, before his works, and his works proved his faith, because they go hand in hand. The just shall live by faith in Christ.

What makes you just, to live by faith? “Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” When you are just, you are keeping God’s laws, and you live by faith in Christ.

That is what Habakkuk is talking about and what Paul is talking about: the just are those who keep God’s commandments, and they shall live by faith.

“If thou wilt, to keep the commandments, and to perform acceptable faithfulness.” If you will keep the commandments, you are to perform acceptable faithfulness. Back to the just shall live by faith.

Keeping God’s commandments is your action, and that action is acceptable faithfulness: that is where your faith lies. Your works prove your faith, and your faith proves your works; they go hand in hand. Keep God’s commandments and you are literally performing faithfulness.

“The fear of the Lord is all wisdom; and in all wisdom is the performance of the law”. The performance of the law is acceptable faithfulness. “And the knowledge of his omnipotency”: God is all around us, and we acknowledge it by keeping his laws.

“Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” Abraham was keeping the commandments.

Obeyed is past tense: it tells what Abraham was doing in the beginning that proved his faith. Abraham heard his voice, kept his charge, his commandments, his statutes and his laws, and that was his acceptable faithfulness.

sense.text: “And the law is not of faith”: not of the promise. The law here is sacrifice, as in Hebrews 9 and Hebrews 10. Abraham’s faith came first; his faith and the promise to him go hand in hand, and the promise predates the law and sacrifice. “The man that doeth them shall live in them.”

“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law”. The curse of the law is condemnation: not being able to atone for every sin, because almost all things, not all, were purged with blood. In the old covenant both houses of Israel went to hell: by standing in the old covenant the whole nation, northern and southern kingdom, was condemned by the law and the prophets. Christ died to take us out of the contract we agreed to in Deuteronomy 27, when all the people said Amen, and put us into a new one.

“Being made a curse for us”: dying for us. The curse and death are the same thing. “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree”: if you broke God’s commandments, often you were hung on the tree. Christ did not break them, but he still died for us.
“That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ”: the Gentiles are the northern kingdom.

precepts.why:
Caiaphas points out what the curse of the law is. “Ye know nothing at all”, “Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.”

Why would the whole nation perish? Because they were under the old covenant they agreed to, and they kept violating it over and over. The northern kingdom went off first, the southern kingdom fell right after, and both were destroyed by the nations. By default both kingdoms were under the curse of the law, condemnation; they should have been destroyed.

But the Lord had other plans: No, I will not destroy them, I love them. I will have my son go and die for them. He redeemed them from that curse.

sense.text: “But before faith came, we were kept under the law”. The we is Israel, the Israelites. Before Christ came on the scene and died for us, we were kept under the law of sacrifice, “shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed”: the same as the carnal ordinances imposed on them until the time of reformation in Hebrews 9.

“Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ”: our mentor, our stepping stone, a placeholder for Christ’s body being offered in the end according to his will and testament, the old testament. “That we might be justified by faith”: justification is in Christ’s death, not in the law of sacrifice, which is no more according to Hebrews 9 and 10.
“But after that faith is come”, now that Christ has come and gone, “we are no longer under a schoolmaster”. The schoolmaster is the law of sacrifice.

“For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus”: ye who were kept under the law, Israel. You are the children of God by faith in Christ now, not by animal sacrifice. That was the bewitching earlier in the chapter: believing you can be justified without Christ, that all you need is an animal.

“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female”. The ye is Israel, the same we that was kept under the law. They were under many different statuses: some were called Jews, some Greeks, some were bond, some free, some male, some female, but they are all the same people of God in Christ.

“And if ye be Christ’s”, if you have faith in Christ and are not bewitched into animal sacrifice, “then are ye Abraham’s seed”: Abraham is the father of faith, so you should be children of faith like your father Abraham. “And heirs according to the promise.” The promise pertains to the Israelites. The Galatians are the children of promise. All nations are not.

If they are, show a nation by its biblical name in the old covenant that God calls his people and to whom the promise pertains alongside Israel. Fill in the blank. Moab? Ammon? The Elamites dropping bombs over there in Israel today? The Canaanites? The Philistines? There is no name.

precepts.why: Some will run with this one: “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance.” See, they will say, there are the names: the Egyptians and the Assyrians. So go a few chapters over and see who the Egypt and Assyria are.

“And ye shall be gathered one by one, O ye children of Israel.” Then “the great trumpet shall be blown”, Christ comes, “and they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt, and shall worship the Lord in the holy mount at Jerusalem.”

So who are my people of Egypt and Assyria? The Israelites who were in those lands.

“The Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.”

Assyria, my people. Egypt, my people. Pathros, still Egypt, my people. Elam: Iran, Pakistan, my people. Shinar: Iraq, my people. Hamath: Syria, my people. The islands of the sea: the Mediterranean, the Caribbean. That is his people, the remnant of Israel in all those places, and it names Assyria and Egypt there.

“And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will bring them again to place them”: that is the second time of Isaiah 11, Judah and Joseph, Judah and Ephraim, all twelve tribes. “For I have mercy upon them: and they shall be as though I had not cast them off”, as though they had never been in captivity.

“I will hiss for them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them”. “I will bring them again also out of the land of Egypt, and gather them out of Assyria”: the same as Isaiah 11:11.

So when he says Egypt my people and Assyria my people, it means Israel in those lands. That is four witnesses, and there is no arguing with it. That is called precepts.

sense.text:
“For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh”: the law here is animal sacrifice. Weak through the flesh means our flesh, and it involves the animals as well.

“God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh”, a man, “and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh”: he did away with death in the flesh, ending our condemnation by his own death on the cross. That is why Caiaphas said it was expedient that one man should die for the people, that the whole nation perish not. He ended the condemnation of all twelve tribes.

precepts.why:
“For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof.” The weakness is the same as Romans 8:3, “in that it was weak”. The commandment that was annulled is sacrifice: for the weakness and the unprofitableness of it, it was done away in Christ.

“For the law made nothing perfect”: it made no man perfect, as Hebrews 10:1 says the sacrifices could not make the comers thereunto perfect. “But the bringing in of a better hope did”: not a what but a who. Christ is the better hope, “by the which we draw nigh unto God.”

So the weakness in Romans 8 is the animal sacrifice that was annulled.

sense.text:
“Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free”: Christ freed us from animal sacrifice. If we had stayed under that we would all be destroyed, because once the temple was destroyed and the priests scattered, how could we atone? You cannot atone for an idolatrous people scattered all over the world. So Christ had to die.

“And be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.” The yoke of bondage is sacrifice, imposed on us until the time of reformation.

“And certain men which came down from Judea taught the brethren”: these certain men are the ones brought in unawares, sent to teach the brethren, the ones who bewitched the Galatians. “Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.” It does not just say circumcised; it says after the manner of Moses, and that difference is very important to understand.
“No small dissension and disputation”: a huge argument.

Verse 5 tells who the certain men of verse 1 are: “certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed”, believed in quotes. The Pharisees made their living by sacrificing, and believing in this Christ was going to take away their money, just like the pastors today. Same exact thing.

“That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses”: keeping the law of Moses here is observing the manner of Moses in circumcision. It is the same thing being said.
“And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.”

“Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples”: the yoke of bondage Christ freed us from in Galatians 5:1. Neither our fathers nor we were able to bear it because the offerings of sacrifices could not make the comers thereunto perfect. We were imperfect, and after a while we started offering up imperfect animals: one eye, three legs, anorexic, no tongue, broken bones, flies all over it. Or we would kill a brother secretly, sleep with his wife, and bring the best goat we had to cover it up. Either the worst animal because we were cheap, or the best to cover our evil, and we still got death regardless, and slavery.

precepts.why:
Here is circumcision after the manner of Moses. “If a woman have conceived seed, and born a man child: then she shall be unclean seven days”. Mary conceived seed and bore a man child, Christ. “And in the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.” After the seven days of her separation, on the eighth day, the child is brought to the temple and circumcised. That is Moses.

She continues “in the blood of her purifying three and thirty days”, forty days for a boy and eighty for a girl, “And when the days of her purifying are fulfilled, for a son, or for a daughter, she shall bring a lamb of the first year for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon, or a turtledove, for a sin offering”. If she cannot bring a lamb, “two turtles, or two young pigeons”.

“This is the law for her that hath born a male or a female.” The sacrifice is for her, and also for the child. Behind the circumcision of Moses comes sacrifice.

“And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS”: the eighth day of Leviticus 12, circumcision after the manner of Moses.

“And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord”, “And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.” The sacrifice is for the woman and the child. So behind circumcision after the manner of Moses comes sacrifice.

“Moses therefore gave unto you circumcision”. See, after the manner of Moses: case closed? No. “Not because it is of Moses, but of the fathers”. Circumcision is not of Moses; it is of Abraham, who was the one circumcised.

So when it says circumcised after the manner of Moses, it is not the same as with Abraham.

“And Abraham was ninety years old and nine, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.” Ninety-nine years old, not eight days. Is that the manner of Moses? No. “And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old”: not the manner of Moses either.

The Pharisees wanted circumcision and sacrifice after the manner of Moses: that was their bread and butter. The more people followed Christ, the more of them stopped sacrificing, and if you stop sacrificing, the Pharisees can’t eat. So they went into the churches saying you have to be circumcised to be saved. That is not what Christ said or what the apostles taught. They were trying to put back on the people the yoke we could not bear.

“For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age”, “And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac being eight days old, as God had commanded him.” This is before Moses. “And Abraham was an hundred years old, when his son Isaac was born unto him.”

Is there any going and sacrificing animals here? No. So this is not after the manner of Moses. There is circumcision after the manner of Moses, and there is the circumcision of the fathers: they are different.

sense.text: “If ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing”: circumcised after the manner of Moses, with the yoke of bondage again. The Pharisees were in there bewitching them, teaching that you must be circumcised and sacrifice an animal to be saved, the hell with Christ. If they are circumcised and believe in the animals, Christ don’t mean nothing to them.

“For I testify again to every man that is circumcised”, after the manner of Moses, “that he is a debtor to do the whole law.” He is indebted to do the whole law. Once that temple was destroyed and the priests scattered, you are done. Go ahead and deal with that if you want to.

“Christ is become of no effect unto you”, because Christ’s sacrifice does away with the animal sacrifice. “Whosoever of you are justified by the law”: animal sacrifice, coupled with circumcision after the manner of Moses, which goes into sacrifice. “Ye are fallen from grace”: if you rely on animals to atone for your sins, you have fallen from the grace Christ got you by dying on the cross. You are rejecting Christ’s sacrifice, being bewitched and simple, running right back to the animals, and you will get yourselves condemned. That is what Paul is saying.

Christians take this verse with Galatians 2:16, 3:2, 3:5 and 3:10-11 and say: see, no commandments, no Sabbath, the hell with that, Christ died for us, we ain’t got to do nothing, just believe. But the law here is sacrifice.

“For as many as have sinned without law shall also perish without law: and as many as have sinned in the law shall be judged by the law”. Whether you die in your ignorance or willfully, you still get death if the Lord so chooses.

“For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified.” Maybe Paul was schizophrenic, writing the letters high on fentanyl? In Galatians he says no man is justified by the works of the law, and here he says the doers of the law shall be justified. So which law justifies you here, and which law in Galatians does not? Here it is the commandments. In Galatians it is the animal sacrifice explained in Hebrews 7:18-19, Hebrews 9 and Hebrews 10, which we are no longer justified by, because Christ did away with it.

You are justified when you keep his commandments. The doers of the law shall be justified: they shall live by their faith, Habakkuk 2:4. Faith had to come first, then the works follow.

precepts.why:
James is Christ’s brother. “Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness”: lay aside all sin. “And receive with meekness the engrafted word”: the word of God, the commandments, the law and the testimony, “which is able to save your souls.” Some say in church that the law can’t save you, only Christ can save you. It is true that Christ saves you, and the law is in Christ: the word of God, keeping God’s commandments, can save your soul.

“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” That goes all the way back to Romans 2:13: the doers of the law shall be justified. Christianity tells you that you don’t have to keep the commandments of God and you still get saved; they deceive themselves, and deceive others in the comments.

The hearer and not a doer “is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass”: “For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.” He reads the Bible and does not apply it: yeah, okay, I’m going to sin some more. He looks in the mirror and forgets what he saw. That is Christianity: believe in God, have faith, and go back to the club, be pimps and drug dealers, hear the Bible, don’t apply it, and pay tithes. Forgetful hearers, not doers that are justified.

“But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty”: Galatians 5:1, Christ freed us and granted us liberty from the yoke of bondage, the yoke of Acts 15 that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear, animal sacrifice. Whoso “continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed”. The work is the commandments, and his deed, his actions, justify him.
What is the engrafted word? “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.” The law and the testimony are the word.

sense.text: “There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus”. The condemnation goes back to the whole nation that should have perished, and to cursed be he that continueth not. Almost all things were purged with blood, not all; if you fell under the almost, you got condemnation, death: stoned to death, set on fire, or hung from a tree. Now there is no condemnation, no death, no cursing to them that have faith in Christ’s death, “who walk not after the flesh”, not in sin, “but after the Spirit.”

“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free”: free is the same as liberty. “From the law of sin and death”: the old law of sacrifice. Under it, if you sinned certain sins against the Lord, you got immediate death. There was no I’m sorry, I repent, I didn’t mean to. There is sin, and there is death.

“For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh”: the law that could not do it is the law of sin and death in verse 2, the same law that was weak in Hebrews 7. It was weak because the people who were offering it were weak and sinful. That is why verse 3 was read first, then back up to verses 1 and 2: it is the same law.

precepts.why:
This shows the law of sin and death. “He that despised Moses’ law died without mercy”. He hated the law we all agreed to keep, and he died without mercy, without grace. There is no grace under Moses: you sin, you get put to death, in most cases.

The Most High had mercy on David, on Moses, on Solomon. But you are not David, you are not Moses, you are not Solomon, you are not Esther. Don’t even try it. Under Mosaic law, a sin you cannot atone for gets death, condemnation. Condemnation and death are the same thing.

sense.text: “Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit”. The letter is the old testament, the Mosaic law of sacrifice; the spirit is Christ, his death. “For the letter killeth”: he that despised Moses’ law died without mercy. The letter, the old covenant sacrifice, gets you condemned and killed, because you could not atone for everything. “But the spirit giveth life”: Christ gives us life. The words that Christ spoke unto us, they are spirit and they are life.

“But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones”: that is Moses. The old covenant is called the ministration of death, the law of sin and death, because if you didn’t keep certain laws you got administered some death. It “was glorious”: those stones of the commandments were glorious.

Moses went up and sat with Christ in the mount forty days and forty nights, and Christ’s glory was on him, “so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance”. He had to wear a veil so Israel could see him and not be blinded. “Which glory was to be done away”: the Mosaic law, the sacrifice.

“How shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious?” The ministration of the spirit is the new testament, the ministration of life: no condemnation in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1. First he called the old the ministration of death; now he calls it “the ministration of condemnation”. “Much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory”: the new covenant is better because under it you can repent of all sins that you could not under the old, where you faced condemnation.

The law of Moses, the sacrifices, the temple, the priests’ dress, the holy of holies, the ephod, the blood sprinkled: all of it was glorious, a sight to behold. But it “had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth”: the ministration of life, Christ’s new testament, because under it everyone can atone for everything they could not under Moses.

“For if that which is done away was glorious”: is done away, not will be. We are under the new covenant now. “Much more that which remaineth is glorious”: the new covenant is better, more glorious.
“Seeing then that we have such hope”, such faith, “we use great plainness of speech”: Paul is writing this very clear and plain to understand.

“And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished”. The glory on Moses’ face symbolised Christ, and the people being blinded by it represented their not being able to see Christ and the old covenant being done away with. That was the blindness of the Pharisees: they were covetous, it was their money, and they were wicked as hell, so they could not see Christ dying on the cross and redeeming us out of animal sacrifice, and they had him killed. Once Christ died their office was done away too, because he became the high priest. The same blindness that fell on our people when Moses came down from the mountain with his face shining is the blindness that kept them from seeing the old covenant done away.

“But their minds were blinded”: they read the Bible and say, Nope, it can’t be, not possible. “For until this day”, until the time Paul wrote, “remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament”: the letter, the ministration of condemnation or death, read by the Pharisees and scribes who cannot understand it. “Which vail is done away in Christ.”

“But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart.” “Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord”, when they repent and acknowledge that Christ is our saviour and died for us, “the vail shall be taken away”: removed from their eyes, from their minds.

“Now the Lord is that Spirit”: Christ is that spirit Moses dealt with, that made him shine. “And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.” Christ has made us free from the law of sin and death: the law of liberty in James. Where Christ is, there is liberty, freedom, atonement for all the things you could not atone for under Moses and animal sacrifice.

precepts.why:
How does the spirit give life? Hebrews 9:22 said almost all things are purged with blood: almost all things you could atone for, if there was an animal for it. But if there was no animal for it, whose blood got shed? Yours. The letter killeth.

“Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins”: that is the life. “And by him all that believe are justified from all things”: not almost, all things, everything you can think of. Christ died for what the animals could not do. You can repent under Christ’s death; under the animals you cannot.

“From which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses”: the law of sacrifice, the law of sin and death, condemnation. That is why Paul said in Galatians that if you want to go by that sacrifice, you are a debtor to do the whole law, including sacrificing animals. And the temple is destroyed: you better figure it out.

“But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.” Where the spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty: that is the perfect law of liberty. Liberty, liberty, liberty.

sense.text: “My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.” Christians love to run to this chapter too, and it is dismantled here. The context is not to be a respecter of persons. When you are a respecter of persons, you are violating loving your neighbour as yourself.

A man comes into the assembly well off, “a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel”, and also “a poor man in vile raiment”. One is fancy, one not so fancy. “The gay clothing” is not gay as in that: it means happy, dressing in expensive clothes. James is addressing a church being respecters of persons. A brother comes in with Gucci on, Prada on: Hey, sit over here, wow. Then the poor brother comes in: Go sit in the corner over there, man, get out of here. James says that is evil as hell. Don’t do that.

“Stand thou there”: just like they say of Christ, standing there all the time with no throne. “Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?” By doing these things you are evil as hell, not examining yourself, not seeing how that is wrong.

“Hearken, my beloved brethren”: listen to me. “Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom”. This nation of Israel as a whole, even now, is poor: poor in spirit and poor in wealth. Very few of our people are wealthy and well off. We are the poor of this world but rich in the faith in Christ; our riches are right here. He is writing to the heirs, and we are the heirs.

“But ye have despised the poor”, by being respecters of persons. “Do not rich men oppress you”: the Pharisees were oppressing them. The white man is rich and he oppresses you too, yet you care about the rich more than the poor, and the rich treat you like garbage. “And draw you before the judgment seats?” The rich Pharisees who hate your guts. “Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by the which ye are called?” The rich Pharisees speak evil of Christ, your master and your saviour.

“If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well”. Remember the context: respect of persons, mistreating the poor for the rich, being partial. The royal law is love your neighbour as yourself.

“But if ye have respect to persons”, if you violate love your neighbour as yourself, “ye commit sin” against the royal law, “and are convinced of the law as transgressors”: guilty, sinners. The law you are convinced of is the royal law, and you broke it.

“For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.” Christians use this to say that if you sin in one law you break them all, so you can’t keep them at all. Stay in context: the whole law here is the whole royal law, love your neighbour as yourself, don’t be a respecter of persons, the rich man and the poor man. The one point is one point of the royal law: thou shalt not bear false witness and the rest, as read in Romans 13.

“For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill”: back to the royal law. If you commit no adultery but kill your brother instead, “thou art become a transgressor of the law”: the royal law.

“So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty.” Under the old covenant, if you violated the moral law, moved your neighbour’s landmark, made the blind wander, slept with your brother’s wife, you got death. Christ redeemed us from that and put us under the law of liberty. So stop doing that.

“For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy”: show no mercy and you shall receive no mercy. “And mercy rejoiceth against judgment”: the Most High chooses to have mercy rather than judge you for violating the royal law.

“What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him?” Faith and works go hand in hand: your faith proves your works and your works prove your faith. It is like a man saying he gets paid tomorrow with no job: the dumbest thing you can say out of your mouth.

“If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food”: back to the royal law, loving your neighbour as yourself. If your works show you treat your poor brother less than your rich brother, you have no faith, because your works show it. To say to a brother with no food and no clothes, “be ye warmed and filled”, makes no damn sense.

“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” In the same way, faith with no works does not exist. Abraham had faith and kept the commandments of God, and by keeping the commandments of God he proved his faith.

“Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works”. In response: “shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.” You cannot show faith without works. You show your faith through your actions, by keeping the commandments of God, as John says in Revelation 14:12 and 22:14, and as Esdras says in 2 Esdras 9:7.

“The devils also believe, and tremble”: even the devils, unclean spirits, believe in God and are afraid. “But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?” The vain man is the follower of Christianity, faith without works: Calvinism, Protestantism, Catholicism.

“Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?” Those were his actions, and his works proved his faith. “Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?” Faith worked with his actions, and by his works his faith was perfected: he was proven faithful. “Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness”, as Galatians 3:6 says, “and he was called the Friend of God.”
“Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.” Back to Romans 2:13: the doers of the law shall be justified.

“Was not Rahab the harlot justified by works”: she believed that if she helped the spies escape, they would spare her life. That was her faith, and helping them was her works, so as not to be killed: “when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way”. She saved them.
“For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.” You have to keep the commandments and the faith of Christ. Each goes with the other.

precepts.why:
What is the royal law? “Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law”: love your neighbour as yourself. “Thou shalt not commit adultery”: royal law. “Thou shalt not kill”: royal law. “Thou shalt not steal”, “Thou shalt not bear false witness”, “Thou shalt not covet”: royal law. “And if there be any other commandment”, outside of those regarding your neighbour, “it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.”

Love your neighbour as yourself is an abbreviation of six of the ten spoken commandments. The first four are how you observe God; the last six are how you serve your neighbour: honour your father and mother, don’t commit adultery, don’t steal, don’t lie, don’t bear false witness. The ten spoken commandments are themselves an abbreviation.

“Love worketh no ill to his neighbour”, like being a respecter of persons does. “Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.” We do it. You simple Christians.

“But when the Pharisees had heard that he had put the Sadducees to silence, they were gathered together.” He had put them to shame. “Then one of them, which was a lawyer, asked him a question, tempting him”. A lawyer is a scribe: their job was copying the scriptures over and over, because the ink fades and the skins rip and smear, so they knew the law and the prophets off the top. He tempted Christ with what he already knew.

“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind”: the first four of the ten spoken commandments. “This is the first and great commandment.” “And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself”: the last six, the royal law.

“On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” They are an abbreviation of all the laws, all of them. Loving God with all your heart, soul and mind means keeping the Sabbath day holy, Passover, Tabernacles, Pentecost, the new moons, the dietary law: don’t drink no blood, don’t eat no pork or shrimp. That is all serving God. The ten are an umbrella over all of them.

Mark gives the same account with more detail, and ties it to sacrifice. In Matthew he is called a lawyer; in Mark, “one of the scribes”, because they wrote things over and over and had the law in their minds. “Which is the first commandment of all?”

“The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength”: the commandments, the dietary law, the civil law, the sacrificial law, all of it is in there. “And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.” If you can keep those, you can keep them all.

“Well, Master, thou hast said the truth”: true, true, true. Then the scribe says: “to love his neighbour as himself, is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” It is better than sacrifices. Mark makes it clear.

Israel would mess around and offer sacrifices, and hate their neighbour, kill their neighbour, steal from their neighbour, sleep with their neighbour’s wife or husband, and offer the best animal. The Lord said, I don’t care about that stuff. I care about your obedience, loving each other, loving me above the animals.

“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” Keeping the commandments is offering enough.

“He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour”: the poor offered fine flour instead of an animal, and requiting a good turn, loving your neighbour as yourself, is that offering. “And he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise.”

“To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation”: mercy, reconciliation.

Saul disobeyed a direct order, and the Lord asks him a question through Samuel: “Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.”

He cares about obedience more than animal sacrifices. That is why Hebrews 10 said sacrifice and burnt offering he would not.

“Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire”: that is what Hebrews 10 quotes. “Mine ears hast thou opened”: David understood in the spirit that the Lord does not really care about sacrifices. David wanted to build the temple, but it was revealed to him: You don’t care about this at all, do you? It is just a placeholder for Christ to show up. Christ was speaking through him, and he realised the Lord cares about obedience, as Samuel told Saul. “Burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.”
“To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice.” Just what he told Saul to do. He says it over and over again.

“Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets”: the word of God can slay; it is the spirit. “And thy judgments are as the light that goeth forth.”

“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” He does not care about that: the sacrifice is a schoolmaster, a placeholder. Through the prophets themselves the Lord eventually said, away with it.

“For all sacrifice is too little for a sweet savour unto thee, and all the fat is not sufficient for thy burnt offering: but he that feareth the Lord is great at all times.” Sacrificing, I don’t care about that. Fearing me and obeying me is more important.

People say, the law can’t save you; you’re not justified by the works of the law. Read it: “And every one that shall be saved, and shall be able to escape by his works, and by faith, whereby ye have believed”. Escape by his works, and by faith.

Works and faith go hand in hand; you have to have both, as James said. You will be saved by both: not faith alone with no works, not faith with no commandments, not commandments with no faith. That makes no sense. It is dead, being alone.

“Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.” Keep the commandments, and the faith of Jesus. The faith is one, and the commandments are the works, as James said and as Esdras said.

“Blessed are they that do his commandments”: do them, deeds, actions, works, “that they may have right to the tree of life”. To enter through the gates into the city they must do the commandments and have faith in Christ. They go hand in hand.
